```{r setup, include = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
# the code of the benchmark is in two scripts in the directory code (one to
# simulate the tracks, one to run the benchmark), from which the chunks below
# are read (purl = FALSE because pkgdown purls this file from the package
# root when looking for images, where these relative paths do not exist)
knitr::read_chunk("code/hr_benchmark_tracks.R")
knitr::read_chunk("code/hr_benchmark.R")
# amt is a suggested package, needed to simulate the example tracks
has_amt <- requireNamespace("amt", quietly = TRUE)
```

`tidytracks`, `amt` (Signer et al. 2019) and `adehabitatHR` (Calenge 2006)
can all estimate home ranges with minimum convex polygons (MCP), kernel
density estimation (KDE) and local convex hulls (LoCoH). This article
compares how long they take, on tracks simulated with `amt` and on copies of
them, and checks that, given the same settings, they give the same home
ranges.

The [results](#results) come first. The second part,
[How the benchmark was run](#how-the-benchmark-was-run), describes the
simulated tracks and the benchmark, with their code, and how to run it again.

# Results

```{r results_packages, include = FALSE}
# to summarise and plot the results
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r read_results, include = FALSE}
# the results of the benchmark, saved by the script in the directory data
area_results <- read.csv("data/hr_benchmark_areas.csv")
timings <- read.csv("data/hr_benchmark_timings.csv")
locoh_scaling <- read.csv("data/hr_benchmark_locoh_scaling.csv")
session <- read.csv("data/hr_benchmark_session.csv")
```

```{r read_areas, include = FALSE}
# the estimators, in the order of the tables and plots
estimator_levels <- c(
  "tidytracks", "tidytracks (binned)", "tidytracks (exact)",
  "amt", "adehabitatHR"
)
# the estimators with which the others are compared
reference_estimators <- c("tidytracks", "tidytracks (exact)")
area_diff <- area_results %>%
  filter(!estimator %in% reference_estimators) %>%
  inner_join(
    area_results %>%
      filter(estimator %in% reference_estimators) %>%
      select(dataset, method, id, level, area_reference = area),
    by = c("dataset", "method", "id", "level")
  ) %>%
  # the relative difference, in %
  mutate(diff = 100 * abs(area / area_reference - 1)) %>%
  group_by(method, estimator, level) %>%
  summarise(
    median_diff = median(diff),
    max_diff = max(diff),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r area_numbers, include = FALSE}
# the largest difference (in %) between the KDE isopleths of an estimator and
# the exact ones of tidytracks, for the text
kde_max_diff <- function(estimator) {
  signif(max(area_diff$max_diff[
    area_diff$method == "kde_iso" & area_diff$estimator == estimator
  ]), 2)
}
```

```{r read_timings, include = FALSE}
# labels for the plots and tables
method_labels <- c(
  mcp = "MCP",
  kde_ud = "KDE: UD",
  kde_iso = "KDE: isopleths",
  locoh = "LoCoH"
)
package_levels <- c("tidytracks", "amt", "adehabitatHR")
timings <- timings %>%
  mutate(
    data_set = paste(
      format(tracks, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE), "tracks of",
      format(locations, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE), "locations"
    ),
    method = factor(method_labels[method], method_labels),
    package = factor(package, package_levels),
    estimator = factor(estimator, estimator_levels)
  )
# the estimators of each method
method_estimators <- distinct(timings, method, package, estimator)
# the packages are compared on the largest data sets (the most copies of the
# tracks), with the estimators that were not run on them
most_copies <- max(timings$copies)
compared <- timings %>%
  filter(copies == most_copies) %>%
  mutate(data_set = factor(data_set, unique(data_set)))
not_run <- compared %>%
  distinct(dataset, data_set) %>%
  cross_join(method_estimators) %>%
  anti_join(compared, by = c("dataset", "method", "estimator"))
```

```{r timing_numbers, include = FALSE}
# the time taken by an estimator on copies of a data set (by default the
# largest), and relative to another estimator (by default tidytracks)
time_of <- function(dataset, method, estimator, copies = most_copies) {
  timings$seconds[
    timings$dataset == dataset &
      timings$method == method_labels[[method]] &
      timings$estimator == estimator &
      timings$copies == copies
  ]
}
ratio <- function(dataset, method, estimator, reference = "tidytracks",
                  copies = most_copies) {
  time_of(dataset, method, estimator, copies) /
    time_of(dataset, method, reference, copies)
}
# a number with 2 significant digits, for the text
fmt <- function(x) {
  trimws(formatC(signif(x, 2), format = "fg", digits = 2, big.mark = ","))
}
# a time, in seconds, or in minutes from a minute, or in hours from an hour
fmt_time <- function(seconds) {
  case_when(
    seconds < 60 ~ paste(fmt(seconds), "s"),
    seconds < 3600 ~ paste(fmt(seconds / 60), "min"),
    TRUE ~ paste(fmt(seconds / 3600), "h")
  )
}
secs <- function(dataset, method, estimator, copies = most_copies) {
  fmt_time(time_of(dataset, method, estimator, copies))
}
# a range of ratios, e.g. "2 to 3", or "2" if they are the same
ratio_range <- function(ratios) {
  ratios <- fmt(range(ratios))
  if (ratios[1] == ratios[2]) {
    ratios[1]
  } else {
    paste(ratios[1], "to", ratios[2])
  }
}
# the ratios of an estimator on the two largest data sets
both_ratios <- function(method, estimator, reference = "tidytracks") {
  ratio_range(c(
    ratio("medium", method, estimator, reference),
    ratio("long", method, estimator, reference)
  ))
}
# the number of tracks and of locations of copies of a data set
size_of <- function(dataset, copies = most_copies, what = "tracks") {
  format(
    unique(timings[[what]][
      timings$dataset == dataset & timings$copies == copies
    ]),
    big.mark = ","
  )
}
binned <- "tidytracks (binned)"
exact <- "tidytracks (exact)"
# the most copies of the medium tracks on which LoCoH was run with
# adehabitatHR
ade_copies <- max(timings$copies[
  timings$package == "adehabitatHR" & timings$method == "LoCoH"
])
# whether the BLAS used is the reference BLAS of R (rather than an optimised
# one, such as OpenBLAS or MKL)
blas <- session$value[session$item == "BLAS"]
reference_blas <- !grepl("openblas|mkl|blis|atlas|accelerate", blas,
  ignore.case = TRUE
)
```

```{r read_scaling, include = FALSE}
locoh_scaling <- locoh_scaling %>%
  mutate(package = factor(package, package_levels))
```

```{r extrapolation, include = FALSE}
# adehabitatHR on its largest track, and extrapolated to the longest track,
# assuming that its time grows with the square of the number of locations
scaling_time <- function(package, locations) {
  locoh_scaling$seconds[
    locoh_scaling$package == package & locoh_scaling$locations == locations
  ]
}
longest <- max(locoh_scaling$locations)
ade_longest <- max(
  locoh_scaling$locations[locoh_scaling$package == "adehabitatHR"]
)
ade_extrapolated <- scaling_time("adehabitatHR", ade_longest) *
  (longest / ade_longest)^2
# adehabitatHR on the long tracks, simulated and in the largest data set
ade_long <- function(copies) {
  n_tracks <- unique(
    timings$tracks[timings$dataset == "long" & timings$copies == copies]
  )
  n_tracks * ade_extrapolated
}
# adehabitatHR on the largest data set of medium tracks, if its time grew in
# proportion to the number of tracks
ade_all_copies <- most_copies / ade_copies *
  time_of("medium", "locoh", "adehabitatHR", ade_copies)
```

```{r plot_functions, include = FALSE}
# one colour per package (and the name of each estimator on the y axis)
package_colours <- c(
  tidytracks = "#2a78d6",
  amt = "#eb6834",
  adehabitatHR = "#1baf7a"
)
# times on a log scale, labelled in seconds, minutes and hours, every factor
# of 10 (in all the plots, which span too many factors of 10 to label every
# factor of about 3)
time_labels <- c(
  "0.01" = "0.01 s", "0.03" = "0.03 s", "0.1" = "0.1 s", "0.3" = "0.3 s",
  "1" = "1 s", "3" = "3 s", "10" = "10 s", "60" = "1 min", "180" = "3 min",
  "600" = "10 min", "1800" = "30 min", "3600" = "1 h"
)
time_breaks <- as.numeric(names(time_labels))
# 0.01 s, 0.1 s, 1 s, 10 s, 1 min, 10 min and 1 h
decades <- c(1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12)
# the limits of an axis of times, at the labels just below and above them
decade_limits <- function(seconds) {
  breaks <- time_breaks[decades]
  c(
    max(breaks[breaks <= min(seconds)]),
    min(breaks[breaks >= max(seconds)])
  )
}
```

## Summary

- Given the same settings, the three packages give the same MCP and LoCoH
  home ranges. The KDE isopleths of `adehabitatHR`, and those of the binned
  method of `tidytracks`, are within about
  `r max(kde_max_diff("adehabitatHR"), kde_max_diff(binned))`% of the exact
  ones of `tidytracks`, and those of `amt` within about
  `r kde_max_diff("amt")`%, as its grid points are not at the centres of the
  cells.
- `tidytracks` is the fastest for LoCoH: on
  `r size_of("long")` tracks of `r size_of("long", what = "locations")`
  locations, it takes `r secs("long", "locoh", "tidytracks")`, against
  `r secs("long", "locoh", "amt")` for `amt`, and `adehabitatHR` takes
  `r secs("medium", "locoh", "adehabitatHR", ade_copies)` on
  `r size_of("medium", ade_copies)` tracks of
  `r size_of("medium", ade_copies, "locations")` locations (against
  `r secs("medium", "locoh", "tidytracks", ade_copies)`). LoCoH in
  `adehabitatHR` becomes impractical beyond a few thousand locations per
  track.
- `tidytracks` is also the fastest for MCP (`amt` and `adehabitatHR` take
  `r both_ratios("mcp", "amt")` and `r both_ratios("mcp", "adehabitatHR")`
  times as long), and, with its default binned method, for the KDE
  isopleths (`amt` and `adehabitatHR` take
  `r both_ratios("kde_iso", "amt", binned)` and
  `r both_ratios("kde_iso", "adehabitatHR", binned)` times as long).
- For the UDs of long tracks, the binned methods of `tidytracks` and `amt`
  are the fastest, `r fmt(ratio("long", "kde_ud", exact, binned))` times
  faster than the exact method of `tidytracks`.

The packages are compared on copies of two sets of tracks simulated with
`amt`: tracks of medium length (`r size_of("medium", 1)` tracks of
`r size_of("medium", 1, "locations")` locations), and long tracks
(`r size_of("long", 1)` tracks of `r size_of("long", 1, "locations")`
locations), with the same settings in all the packages. The largest data
sets have `r most_copies` copies of these tracks (see
[The data sets](#the-data-sets) and
[Running the estimators](#running-the-estimators)).

## Do the packages give the same home ranges?

For each method, data set and level, we compare the area of the home range of
each simulated track from each estimator with the area from `tidytracks`
(with its exact method, for the KDE):

```{r table_areas, echo = FALSE}
area_diff %>%
  mutate(
    method = recode(
      method,
      mcp = "MCP",
      kde_iso = "KDE",
      locoh = "LoCoH"
    ),
    level = paste0(100 * level, "%"),
    across(
      c(median_diff, max_diff),
      ~ case_when(
        .x == 0 ~ "0",
        .x < 0.001 ~ "< 0.001",
        TRUE ~ formatC(signif(.x, 2), format = "fg", digits = 2)
      )
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(
    match(method, c("MCP", "KDE", "LoCoH")),
    match(estimator, estimator_levels),
    level
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Method", "Estimator", "Level",
      "Median difference (%)", "Largest difference (%)"
    ),
    align = "lllrr"
  )
```

MCP and LoCoH give the same home ranges in all three packages (the tiny
differences for LoCoH in `amt` come from its buffering of each hull by
0.00001 m). For the KDE, the isopleths of `adehabitatHR` are within
`r kde_max_diff("adehabitatHR")`% of the exact ones of `tidytracks`: both
evaluate the same kernels at the same points, and differ only in how they
draw the isopleths from the UDs. The binned estimators approximate the KDE,
as binning moves each location by less than a cell: the binned isopleths of
`tidytracks` are within `r kde_max_diff("tidytracks (binned)")`% of the exact
ones, and those of `amt` within `r kde_max_diff("amt")`%. Both bin the
locations in the same way, and smooth them with the same kernel, but `amt`
(with `KernSmooth::bkde2D()`) estimates the density at
grid points that go from edge to edge of its raster, rather than at the
centres of its cells: they are slightly more than a cell apart, so its UD is
stretched by up to half a cell towards the edges of the grid.

## How long do they take?

On the largest data sets (`r most_copies` copies of the simulated tracks):

```{r plot_timings, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6.5}
ggplot(compared, aes(x = seconds, y = estimator, colour = package)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  # the estimators that were not run on these data sets
  geom_text(
    data = not_run,
    aes(x = sqrt(prod(range(compared$seconds))), label = "not run"),
    colour = "grey40",
    size = 3
  ) +
  # each method with its own estimators
  facet_grid(method ~ data_set, scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = time_breaks[decades],
    labels = time_labels[decades],
    limits = decade_limits(compared$seconds)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = package_colours, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Time (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing.x = unit(2, "lines"),
    strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0),
    panel.border = element_rect(
      colour = "grey70",
      fill = NA,
      linewidth = 0.5
    )
  )
```

```{r table_timings, echo = FALSE}
# one column per package, plus one for the exact KDE of tidytracks (the
# column of tidytracks has its default, binned, KDE), for all the data sets
table_columns <- c("tidytracks", "tidytracks (exact)", "amt", "adehabitatHR")
timings %>%
  # the medium tracks first, from the fewest copies to the most
  arrange(match(dataset, c("medium", "long")), copies) %>%
  mutate(
    column = recode(
      as.character(estimator),
      "tidytracks (binned)" = "tidytracks"
    ),
    column = factor(column, table_columns),
    data_set = factor(data_set, unique(data_set))
  ) %>%
  select(data_set, method, column, seconds) %>%
  arrange(column) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = column, values_from = seconds) %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      all_of(table_columns),
      ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), "not run", fmt_time(.x))
    ),
    # tidytracks only has an exact method for the KDE
    `tidytracks (exact)` = ifelse(
      grepl("KDE", method),
      `tidytracks (exact)`,
      ""
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(data_set, method) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Data set", "Method", "tidytracks", "tidytracks (exact KDE)", "amt",
      "adehabitatHR"
    ),
    align = "llrrrr",
    caption = paste(
      "Time to estimate the home ranges of all the tracks, on the simulated",
      "tracks and their copies. For the KDE, the column tidytracks is for",
      "its default, binned, method."
    )
  )
```

- **MCP** takes at most
  `r fmt_time(max(compared$seconds[compared$method == "MCP"]))` in all three
  packages. `tidytracks` is the fastest: `amt` takes
  `r fmt(ratio("medium", "mcp", "amt"))` times as long on the medium tracks,
  and `adehabitatHR` `r fmt(ratio("medium", "mcp", "adehabitatHR"))` times
  (`r fmt(ratio("long", "mcp", "adehabitatHR"))` times on the long tracks).
- **KDE**: the exact estimators (`tidytracks` with `method = "exact"`, and
  `adehabitatHR`) evaluate the kernel of every location in every cell of the
  grid, which takes a time proportional to the number of locations times the
  number of cells, whilst the binned estimators (`tidytracks` with its
  default, `method = "binned"`, and `amt`) first bin the locations onto the
  grid, so that their time hardly depends on the number of locations. On the
  long tracks, the binned estimators are thus much faster: the UDs take
  `r secs("long", "kde_ud", binned)` with `tidytracks` and
  `r secs("long", "kde_ud", "amt")` with `amt`, against
  `r secs("long", "kde_ud", exact)` with the exact method of `tidytracks`
  (`r fmt(ratio("long", "kde_ud", exact, binned))` times as long) and
  `r secs("long", "kde_ud", "adehabitatHR")` with `adehabitatHR`. On the
  medium tracks, which have fewer locations each, the time is mostly spent
  on building the UD of each track: `tidytracks` takes
  `r secs("medium", "kde_ud", binned)` (`r secs("medium", "kde_ud", exact)`
  with its exact method), `amt` `r secs("medium", "kde_ud", "amt")` and
  `adehabitatHR` `r secs("medium", "kde_ud", "adehabitatHR")`. Drawing the
  isopleths of the medium tracks adds little to the time of `tidytracks`,
  which draws them straight from the UDs, without building rasters
  (`r fmt_time(time_of("medium", "kde_iso", binned) - time_of("medium", "kde_ud", binned))`
  with the binned method), but
  `r fmt_time(time_of("medium", "kde_iso", "amt") - time_of("medium", "kde_ud", "amt"))`
  to that of `amt`, and
  `r fmt_time(time_of("medium", "kde_iso", "adehabitatHR") - time_of("medium", "kde_ud", "adehabitatHR"))`
  to that of `adehabitatHR`. From the locations to the isopleths, the binned
  method of `tidytracks` is thus the fastest on both data sets: `amt` takes
  `r both_ratios("kde_iso", "amt", binned)` times as long, and
  `adehabitatHR` `r both_ratios("kde_iso", "adehabitatHR", binned)` times.
  Most of the time of the exact method of `tidytracks` on long tracks is
  spent in a matrix product (in `MASS::kde2d()`), which an optimised BLAS
  (such as OpenBLAS) can make several times faster, as it can the matrix
  products of the binned method; this benchmark used
  `r if (reference_blas) "the reference BLAS of R" else paste0("an optimised BLAS (", blas, ")")`.
- **LoCoH**: `tidytracks` is the fastest, by far: `amt` takes
  `r both_ratios("locoh", "amt")` times as long
  (`r secs("long", "locoh", "amt")` on the `r size_of("long")` long tracks,
  against `r secs("long", "locoh", "tidytracks")`). `LoCoH.k()` from
  `adehabitatHR` was only run on the `r size_of("medium", ade_copies)`
  simulated medium tracks, on which it takes
  `r fmt(ratio("medium", "locoh", "adehabitatHR", copies = ade_copies))`
  times as long as `tidytracks`
  (`r secs("medium", "locoh", "adehabitatHR", ade_copies)`, against
  `r secs("medium", "locoh", "tidytracks", ade_copies)`): it would take
  about `r fmt_time(ade_all_copies)` on their `r most_copies` copies, and
  `r fmt_time(ade_long(most_copies))` on the `r size_of("long")` long tracks
  (see below).

## LoCoH on a single track

```{r plot_scaling, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
ggplot(locoh_scaling, aes(x = locations, y = seconds, colour = package)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  # each line labelled at its last point
  geom_text(
    data = locoh_scaling %>%
      group_by(package) %>%
      filter(locations == max(locations)),
    aes(label = package),
    hjust = 0,
    # in log10 units, as the x axis is on a log scale
    nudge_x = 0.06,
    colour = "grey20",
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000),
    labels = c("500", "1,000", "2,000", "5,000", "10,000"),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.3))
  ) +
  scale_y_log10(
    breaks = time_breaks[decades],
    labels = time_labels[decades]
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = package_colours) +
  labs(
    x = "Locations (log scale)",
    y = "Time (log scale)",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "top")
```

The time taken by `tidytracks` and `amt` grows about linearly with the
number of locations, whilst that of `adehabitatHR`, which computes the
distances between all pairs of locations (in R), roughly quadruples each time
the number of locations doubles: it takes
`r fmt_time(scaling_time("adehabitatHR", ade_longest))` on
`r format(ade_longest, big.mark = ",")` locations (on 5,000 locations, it
stopped after several minutes, as it ran out of protection stack, even with
the largest one that R allows). A track of
`r format(longest, big.mark = ",")` locations would thus take it about
`r fmt_time(ade_extrapolated)`, and the `r size_of("long")` long tracks of
the largest data set about `r fmt_time(ade_long(most_copies))`, against
`r fmt_time(scaling_time("tidytracks", longest))` per track for
`tidytracks`.

# How the benchmark was run

The benchmark takes about
`r round(as.numeric(session$value[session$item == "run time (minutes)"]) / 10) * 10`
minutes to run, so it was run once with the script
`vignettes/articles/code/hr_benchmark.R` (in the source code of the
package), and its results are read here from the directory
`vignettes/articles/data`. It uses tracks simulated beforehand with the
script `vignettes/articles/code/hr_benchmark_tracks.R`, and stored in the
same directory, so it can be run again (e.g. on another machine) without
simulating them. The code shown below is taken from these two scripts.
Timings depend on the machine (see
[Machine and software](#machine-and-software)), but the differences between
the packages, and how the times grow with the size of the data, should be
similar on other machines.

The benchmark uses these packages:

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
```

## Simulating tracks with amt

`amt` can simulate movement from an integrated step selection function
(iSSF; Avgar et al. 2016), which combines a movement kernel (the
distributions of step lengths and turning angles) with the selection of
the places where steps end. To get tracks that stay within a home range,
the selection decreases with the squared distance from a centre:

```{r simulate-track, eval = has_amt}
```

For example, the first three tracks of the first data set below:

```{r example_tracks, eval = has_amt}
example_tracks <- lapply(1:3, function(i) {
  simulate_track(
    id = sprintf("medium_%03d", i),
    n_locations = 500,
    seed = 1000 + i
  )
})
example_tracks <- do.call(rbind, example_tracks)
```

```{r plot_example_tracks, eval = has_amt, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3}
ggplot(example_tracks, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_path(colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~id) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Easting (m)", y = "Northing (m)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

## The data sets

We simulate two sets of tracks, with the same model: tracks of medium
length, and fewer, longer tracks (with one location per hour, about three
weeks and fourteen months of tracking respectively):

```{r simulate-datasets, eval = FALSE}
```

Simulating the tracks takes about 8 minutes on 4 cores: each step takes
about 10 ms, mostly in the bookkeeping of `amt` rather than in the simulation
itself. So the tracks were simulated once (with
`code/hr_benchmark_tracks.R`) and stored in `data/hr_benchmark_tracks.rds`,
from which the benchmark reads them:

```{r read-tracks, eval = FALSE}
```

The home ranges are estimated on these tracks, and on copies of them:

```{r copies, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r table_data_sets, echo = FALSE}
timings %>%
  distinct(dataset, copies, data_set) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = dataset, values_from = data_set) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Copies", "Medium tracks", "Long tracks"),
    align = "rll",
    caption = "The data sets."
  )
```

## Running the estimators

Each package works on its own class of objects: a `move2` object for
`tidytracks`, a `track_xy` for `amt` and a `SpatialPointsDataFrame` (from
`sp`) for `adehabitatHR`. These are built from the data frame of each data
set (outside of the timings):

```{r inputs, eval = FALSE}
```

The KDEs are estimated on the same grid for all the packages:

```{r grid, eval = FALSE}
```

The home ranges are then estimated with each method and package, at the 50%
and 95% levels, and with both of the methods of `tidytracks` for the KDE (see
below). `tidytracks` and `adehabitatHR` estimate the home ranges of all the
tracks in one call; `amt` estimates the home range of a single track, so its
estimators are applied to each track in turn, after nesting the tracks as
shown in the documentation of `amt`:

```{r estimators, eval = FALSE}
```

The settings are matched so that the packages estimate the same home ranges:

- **MCP**: all three packages exclude the locations farthest from the mean
  of the locations, and build the convex hull of the others.
- **KDE**: all three use a bivariate normal kernel, with the reference
  bandwidth of each track (\(h = \sqrt{(\sigma^2_x + \sigma^2_y)/2} \, n^{-1/6}\)),
  on the same grid. The UDs are timed on their own (`kde_ud`), and with
  their isopleths (`kde_iso`, i.e. from the locations to the isopleths).
  The UD on a grid can be estimated in two ways. The exact estimators
  evaluate the kernel of every location at the centre of every cell: those
  of `adehabitatHR`, and of `tidytracks` with `method = "exact"` (which uses
  `MASS::kde2d()`). The binned estimators first bin the locations onto the
  grid (splitting each location between the four cells whose centres
  surround it), and then smooth the bin counts with the kernel, which is
  faster but approximate: those of `amt` (with `KernSmooth::bkde2D()`, which
  smooths them with fast Fourier transforms), and of `tidytracks` with
  `method = "binned"`, its default (which bins the locations as
  `KernSmooth::bkde2D()` does, but smooths them with two matrix products, one
  along each axis of the grid, as the Gaussian kernel is separable).
- **LoCoH**: hulls of each location and its 10 nearest neighbours (`n = 10`
  in `tidytracks` and `amt`, `k = 11` in `adehabitatHR`, which counts the
  location itself). For each level, the isopleth is the union of the
  smallest hulls whose coverage (the proportion of locations in the hulls)
  is closest to the level.

Each estimator is run once, on an otherwise idle machine, and on a single
performance core of its CPU (see
[Running the benchmark again](#running-the-benchmark-again)); the estimators
that take long are timed precisely enough by a single run:

```{r timing, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r run-benchmark, eval = FALSE}
```

The areas of the home ranges of the simulated tracks (whose copies give the
same home ranges) are then extracted from the results of each package (with
the functions in `areas`, in the script). `LoCoH.k()` from `adehabitatHR` is
only run on the simulated medium tracks: it would take about
`r fmt_time(ade_all_copies)` on their copies, and
`r fmt_time(ade_long(1))` on the simulated long tracks alone (see
[LoCoH on a single track](#locoh-on-a-single-track)).

The benchmark saves its results in `data/hr_benchmark_*.csv`, which are read
and summarised for the [results](#results) above with this code:

```{r, ref.label = c("results_packages", "read_results", "read_areas", "read_timings", "read_scaling"), eval = FALSE}
```

and the plots of the timings are drawn with:

```{r, ref.label = c("plot_functions", "plot_timings", "plot_scaling"), eval = FALSE}
```

## Running the benchmark again

To run the benchmark again (e.g. after changing `tidytracks`, or on another
machine), install `tidytracks` (with `R CMD INSTALL`, rather than loading it
with `devtools::load_all()`, which compiles its C++ code without
optimisation), `amt`, `adehabitatHR` and `sp`, and run, on an otherwise idle
machine (with a larger protection stack than the default, which
`adehabitatHR` exceeds when it builds the polygons of LoCoH on thousands of
locations):

```sh
cd vignettes/articles
taskset -c 4 Rscript --max-ppsize=500000 code/hr_benchmark.R
```

which overwrites `data/hr_benchmark_*.csv`; then render this article again.
`taskset -c 4` (on Linux) runs R on core 4 only: on a CPU with performance
and efficiency cores, such as the Intel i9-13900 used here, the efficiency
cores are almost half as fast, and R could otherwise move from one kind of
core to the other during the benchmark, which would change the times of some
estimators more than others. Use one of the performance cores (`lscpu -e`
lists the cores, with their maximum frequency), or drop `taskset -c 4` on a
CPU whose cores are all the same.

`Rscript code/hr_benchmark.R quick` runs everything on the first locations of
a few tracks, to check the script, and saves its results in a temporary
directory instead. The simulated tracks are only needed again for
a different simulation: `Rscript code/hr_benchmark_tracks.R` simulates them
and overwrites `data/hr_benchmark_tracks.rds`.
